title: Multiple catch & Exception Flow
summary: Master multiple catch blocks, catch ordering rules, stack unwinding across the Call Stack, nested try-catch blocks, and rethrowing exceptions.
learningOutcomes: Implement multi-branch exception handling with tailored recovery logic
Trace stack unwinding as unhandled exceptions bubble through method calls

activities.title: Core Mechanics: Multiple catch & Exception Flow

breakdown.details: Sequential evaluation: JVM executes the first matching block and skips the rest.
Child classes must strictly precede parent classes to avoid unreachable code compile errors.
Popping stack frames in reverse call order until a matching catch block is found on the Call Stack.
A catch block can capture an exception, perform local logging, and rethrow it using throw e; for higher-level handling.

activities.description: Demonstrates multiple catch block matching, scenario switching, and finally block execution.

steps.description: Block 2 catches Scenario 1; Blocks 1, 3, and 4 are skipped.
Scenario 3 throws NumberFormatException, caught by Block 3.
Finally executes after every single scenario, ensuring teardown.

activities.title: Concept Check & MCQ: Multiple catch & Exception Flow

questions.question: In a try block with multiple catch blocks, how many catch blocks can execute for a single thrown exception?
options: All catch blocks that match the type
At most ONE matching catch block executes
Two catch blocks: the specific and the general
None, catch blocks only execute after finally
questions.explanation: The JVM evaluates catch blocks sequentially from top to bottom. As soon as the first matching catch block is found, it executes, and all remaining catch blocks are skipped.

questions.question: What is 'Stack Unwinding' in Java exception processing?
options: A tool to optimize CPU registers
The process of removing method stack frames from the Call Stack as an unhandled exception propagates up to caller methods
A garbage collector algorithm for arrays
questions.explanation: Stack unwinding occurs when an exception is not caught in the method where it was thrown: the JVM pops the current frame and searches the caller frame, repeating until a handler is found or the thread terminates.

questions.question: What is the result of placing `catch (Exception e)` BEFORE `catch (IOException e)`?
options: The code fails to compile with an 'unreachable catch block' error
The JVM prints a warning at runtime
questions.explanation: Since IOException is a subclass of Exception, the first block would catch all IOExceptions, making the second block unreachable. The compiler flags this as an error.
In `arr[5] = 10 / 0;`, the right-hand side expression `10 / 0` evaluates BEFORE the array assignment occurs. Division by zero throws `ArithmeticException` first, so "A" prints.

questions.question: Can a `catch` block rethrow the exact same exception it caught using `throw e;`?
options: No, once an exception is caught, it cannot be thrown again
Yes, rethrowing an exception allows local logging while delegating recovery to higher layers
Only if e is cast to RuntimeException
questions.explanation: Rethrowing (`throw e;`) is a standard architectural pattern where an intermediate layer logs diagnostic details and re-raises the exception for upstream handling.

questions.question: What happens if an exception is thrown inside a `catch` block while handling another exception?
options: The new exception immediately interrupts the catch block and begins propagating up the call stack
Both exceptions merge into a hybrid exception
The program ignores the new exception
questions.explanation: An exception thrown inside a catch block interrupts that catch block immediately and propagates outward to any enclosing try-catch or caller method.

questions.question: Can try-catch blocks be nested inside another try block?
options: No, Java forbids nested try blocks
Yes, try blocks can be nested to handle specific inner errors independently
questions.explanation: Nested try-catch blocks are fully supported in Java, enabling granular local recovery before affecting the outer block.
The inner catch expects NullPointerException, but ArithmeticException was thrown. The inner catch does not match, so the exception propagates to the outer catch, printing "Outer".

questions.question: In multi-catch syntax `catch (ArithmeticException | NumberFormatException e)`, how many catch blocks are created in bytecode?
options: A single catch block in source code that generates a shared bytecode handler
questions.explanation: Multi-catch generates a single shared handler block in bytecode, avoiding code duplication across identical handlers.

questions.question: What happens if a method encounters an exception and has a `finally` block but no matching `catch` block?
options: The finally block executes completely, and then the exception continues propagating up the call stack
questions.explanation: Even without a matching catch block, `finally` executes before the method's stack frame is popped during stack unwinding.

activities.title: Interview Q&A: Multiple catch & Exception Flow

interviewQA.question: What is the order of execution in a try block with multiple catch blocks?
interviewQA.answer: When an exception is thrown in the try block, the JVM examines the catch blocks sequentially from top to bottom. The first catch block whose declared parameter type matches the thrown exception (is assignable from it) executes. Once that catch block finishes, all remaining catch blocks are bypassed.

interviewQA.question: What is Stack Unwinding and how does Java perform it?
interviewQA.answer: Stack unwinding is the runtime process of searching for an exception handler across the Call Stack. If the method where the exception occurred lacks a matching catch block, that method's stack frame is popped, and the exception is propagated to the calling method. This repeats up the stack until a matching catch block is found or the main thread terminates.

interviewQA.question: Why would an engineer rethrow an exception using 'throw e' in a catch block?
interviewQA.answer: Rethrowing is used when the current method can only partially handle the error (e.g. logging an audit record, rolling back a local transaction, or freeing local resources), but the higher-level caller must still be notified that the business operation failed so it can alert the user or redirect the request.

interviewQA.question: What is Exception Chaining (wrapping) and why is it preferred over throwing a new exception directly?
interviewQA.answer: Exception chaining is wrapping a lower-level exception inside a higher-level domain exception (e.g. `throw new OrderProcessingException("Order failed", sqlException)`). Passing the lower-level exception as the `cause` preserves the original root-cause stack trace, allowing engineers to diagnose the underlying technical failure in logs.

interviewQA.question: Can an exception thrown in an inner try block be caught by the outer catch block?
interviewQA.answer: Yes. If an exception occurs in an inner `try` block and the inner `catch` blocks do not match its type, the exception immediately bubbles out to the enclosing outer `try-catch` structure.

interviewQA.question: What happens if both the try block and the finally block throw an exception?
interviewQA.answer: If an exception is in-flight from the `try` block and another exception is thrown inside `finally`, the exception from `finally` takes precedence and propagates upward. In pre-Java 7, the original exception was lost. In Java 7+ try-with-resources, secondary exceptions are recorded as **Suppressed Exceptions** on the primary exception (`e.getSuppressed()`).

interviewQA.question: Why does Java enforce that child exceptions must precede parent exceptions in multiple catch blocks?
interviewQA.answer: Because polymorphism dictates that an instance of a child class `is-a` parent class. If `catch (Exception e)` were placed above `catch (IOException e)`, the first block would match all `IOExceptions`, leaving the second block completely dead (unreachable). The compiler rejects unreachable code at compile-time.

practiceProblems.title: Build Multi-Branch Exception Handler
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Write a method `handleInput(String text)`: inside try, parse integer and divide 100 by that integer. Catch `NumberFormatException` printing "Bad Format", catch `ArithmeticException` printing "Divide By Zero", and finally print "Done". Test with text = "0".
practiceProblems.description: Write a method `handleInput(String text)`: inside try, parse integer and divide 100 by that integer. Catch `NumberFormatException` printing "Bad Format", catch `ArithmeticException` printing "Divide By Zero", and finally print "Done". Test with text = "0".
practiceProblems.hint: Catch NumberFormatException and ArithmeticException in separate blocks.
hints: Catch NumberFormatException and ArithmeticException in separate blocks.

practiceProblems.title: Trace Stack Unwinding Across Three Methods
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Create three methods: `methodC()` throws `ArithmeticException (10 / 0)`. `methodB()` calls `methodC()`. `methodA()` calls `methodB()` inside try-catch. `main` calls `methodA()`. Catch the exception in `methodA()` and print "Handled in methodA via unwinding".
practiceProblems.description: Create three methods: `methodC()` throws `ArithmeticException (10 / 0)`. `methodB()` calls `methodC()`. `methodA()` calls `methodB()` inside try-catch. `main` calls `methodA()`. Catch the exception in `methodA()` and print "Handled in methodA via unwinding".
practiceProblems.hint: Exception bubbles up from C to B to A.
hints: Exception bubbles up from C to B to A.

practiceProblems.title: Rethrow an Exception for Higher-Level Logging
practiceProblems.problemStatement: In method `processPayment(double amount)`, if `amount <= 0`, catch `IllegalArgumentException` triggered by `throw new IllegalArgumentException("Negative amount")`, print "Audit: Invalid amount logged", and rethrow it (`throw e;`). In `main`, call `processPayment(-50)` and catch the rethrown exception, printing "Payment Rejected".
